Petrarchan sonnet.note: Eight opening lines and a six-line response; line 9 is the conventional turn. CDECDE and CDCDCD are common sestet patterns. The diagram shows the CDECDE option.

edges.evidence: The opening division contains eight lines. This uses the generic octave sense only; the specifically octosyllabic huitain scheme is not a requirement.
The answering division is six lines; the generic sestet sense applies independently of its particular rhyme order.
The derived form is Miltonic sonnet. Its outgoing assertion supplies the specific-to-general direction. Treating Petrarchan sonnet as the variant would reverse that direction.

Sicilian sonnet.note: The row specifies an alternating octave and two sestet options. These model the catalog entry; the historical Sicilian school does not reduce to a single specimen. The diagram illustrates one of the two sestet choices.

edges.evidence: The opening division contains eight lines. This uses the generic octave sense only; the specifically octosyllabic huitain scheme is not a requirement.
The answering division is six lines; the generic sestet sense applies independently of its particular rhyme order.
Both catalog entries have an octave followed by a sestet; their opening rhyme patterns differ.
The opening ABABABAB realizes the catalogued Sicilian octave scheme. Shared structure alone does not establish historical descent.

Miltonic sonnet.note: The sentence may cross the boundary between octave and sestet, delaying or softening the expected turn.

edges.evidence: The opening division contains eight lines. This uses the generic octave sense only; the specifically octosyllabic huitain scheme is not a requirement.
The answering division is six lines; the generic sestet sense applies independently of its particular rhyme order.
The documented parent structure is the Petrarchan octave and sestet.

Shakespearean sonnet.note: The three alternating-rhyme quatrains are followed by a rhyming pair. Those divisions need not be printed as four stanzas.

edges.evidence: Three four-line rhyme groups make up the first twelve lines.
The final two metrical lines share a rhyme distinct from the preceding quatrains.

Spenserian sonnet.note: The last rhyme sound of each of the first two quatrains starts the next. A new EE pair closes.

edges.evidence: Three four-line rhyme groups make up the first twelve lines.
The final two metrical lines share a rhyme distinct from the preceding quatrains.
The adaptation connects successive quatrains with shared rhyme sounds before the closing couplet.

Terza rima sonnet.note: Four three-line units interlock by their middle rhyme, and the final couplet resolves the chain. Four tercets belong to this sonnet version, not to all terza rima.

edges.evidence: The sonnet specializes interlocking terza rima to four tercets and a two-line close.
The final EE uses two rhyming lines to resolve the last tercet.
Its first twelve lines are four actual three-line groups.

Curtal sonnet.note: Six lines answer to the Italian octave and four and a half to its sestet. An abbreviated final line occupies the eleventh printed position.

edges.evidence: The Italian ratio of eight lines to six is reduced proportionally to six lines and four and a half.
The six opening lines form one six-line division.
Two ABC tercets constitute the six-line opening.

Caudate sonnet.note: A complete sonnet precedes one or more tails. In the catalog version each tail starts with a shortened line followed by two full lines.

edges.evidence: Each added tail appends two rhyming full lines to a shortened line.
In the catalog construction, a short line and two full lines form each three-line tail.

Meredithian sonnet.note: Four enclosed-rhyme units span sixteen lines. They can be printed continuously.

edges.evidence: The sixteen lines make four enclosed four-line rhyme groups.

Onegin stanza.note: Fourteen iambic tetrameter lines use ABAB CCDD EFFE GG. In the diagram’s local legend, lowercase marks a trailing unstressed syllable and capitals mark a stressed ending: aBaB ccDD eFFe GG.

edges.evidence: The stanza is attested as the recurring unit of a verse novel. Other verse novels can use different units.
The final rhyming tetrameter pair closes the stanza.
Three four-line rhyme groups precede the final pair. These units can share one printed stanza.

Bref double.note: Three quatrains and two closing lines on separate a and b rhymes. The catalog specifies the c-ending version. Individual a/b positions in the quatrains are unspecified.

edges.evidence: Three four-line stanzas precede the ending.
The closing two-line unit pairs the separate returning a and b rhyme sounds by design.

Sonnenizio.note: One word from the borrowed opening recurs in the thirteen succeeding lines. The final two lines also rhyme.

edges.evidence: The last two lines are a rhymed ending in the published form definition.

American sonnet.note: Fourteen lines and a turn are useful reference points, but contemporary practice allows both shape and rhyme to vary; no single tree fits every example.

Duplex.note: Seven couplets form fourteen lines of nine to eleven syllables. The second line of each of the first six pairs echoes at the next opening, and the last line echoes the first.

edges.evidence: The duplex draws on the ghazal’s two-line stanza organization.
The fourteen-line poem is organized into seven intentional two-line stanzas.
A line from one stanza recurs in the next. The echo in the duplex may vary, and the two forms transfer different positions.
The repeated and varied line draws on A–A′–B blues lyrics. This link concerns verbal repetition, with no requirement for twelve musical bars.

Kyrielle sonnet.note: The catalog’s two refrain lines are ambiguous. In the cited specimen the first and last lines of quatrain one make the closing pair; the latter alone ends every preceding quatrain.

edges.evidence: The quatrains keep the returning final line of a kyrielle.
The form has three four-line stanzas before its ending.
After the three quatrains, the opening line and the repeated refrain form a distinct two-line close.

Crown of sonnets.note: Each last line opens the next sonnet, and the final line returns to the first. The number of sonnets can vary.

edges.evidence: A crown is a sequence whose neighboring sonnets share boundary lines and whose ending closes the loop.

Heroic crown.note: The first fourteen form a closed crown. Their opening lines in sequence form the fifteenth, or master, sonnet.

edges.evidence: The first fourteen form a corona. The fifteenth collects their opening lines.

Sonnet sequence.note: A series of sonnets develops a subject or progression. Some sequences use verbal linkage: in a crown, each closing line opens the next sonnet and the cycle returns to its beginning.

Villanelle.note: In the fixed 19-line form the two opening refrains alternate across four tercets. They meet inside the closing quatrain, rather than forming an extra two-line stanza.

edges.evidence: The first fifteen lines make five tercets.
The two refrain lines close a four-line final stanza.
The final two lines are the two opening refrains deliberately brought together within the closing quatrain.

Terzanelle.note: In the 19-line pattern each middle line becomes the final line of the next tercet. The opening pair of refrains returns in the closing quatrain; it does not alternate through the body as in a villanelle.

edges.evidence: Five tercets lead to a quatrain, with two opening refrain lines recalled at the end.
Successive tercets interlock their rhyme sounds as in terza rima.
The traditional nineteen-line design opens with five three-line stanzas.
Its four-line ending collects the opening refrains.

Sestina.note: Labels 1–6 stand for end-words, not rhymes. Each stanza takes the prior positions in the order 6,1,5,2,4,3; the three-line envoi uses all six words.

edges.evidence: The six full stanzas have six lines each; rhyme is not implied by this generic sestet relationship.
The final envoi has three lines.

Double sestina.note: Two attested constructions differ in both stanza size and envoi. Twelve stanzas of twelve end in six lines; twelve stanzas of six end in three.

edges.evidence: Both documented doubled variants adapt the sestina’s permuted end-words and concluding envoi.
The 75-line construction ends in a three-line envoi.
The 75-line construction uses twelve six-line stanzas. The 150-line construction has a six-line envoi.

Tritina.note: Three end-words rotate through three tercets in the orders ABC, CAB and BCA. A single final line gathers all three.

edges.evidence: Its three end-word rotations occupy three-line stanzas.
The shorter adaptation reduces the rotating end-word inventory from six to three and gathers them in one final line.
A one-line envoi is part of a longer poem. The catalog defines monostich as a complete one-line poem.

Rondeau.note: Fifteen positions group 5 + 4 + 6. R is a returning phrase from the opening, not a third rhyme class.

edges.evidence: The derived form is Rondine. Its outgoing assertion supplies the specific-to-general direction. Treating Rondeau as the variant would reverse that direction.
The derived form is Rondeau prime. Its outgoing assertion supplies the specific-to-general direction. Treating Rondeau as the variant would reverse that direction.
The common 15-line rondeau opens with five lines.
Its second stanza contains four lines including the short return.
Its third stanza contains six lines including the short return.

Rondeau prime.note: The documented twelve-position setting divides into a septet and a quintain, abbaabR / abbaR. The returning opening fragment occupies positions seven and twelve. Historical naming can depend on the particular refrain treatment.

edges.evidence: The named shorter rondeau variant brings the opening fragment back at stanza endings.
Both names are documented for twelve-position arrangements with matching stanza lengths and rhyme letters. Refrain treatment and historical terminology limit interchangeability.
The twelve-position setting opens with seven positions, including its returning phrase.
The closing five positions include the shortened refrain.
The uncorroborated thirteen-position inventory outline supplied this link. The attested setting closes with five positions.

Rondine.note: Six full lines and a short refrain make the opening septet, abbaabR. Four full lines and the returning fragment make the closing quintain, abbaR.

edges.evidence: The short adaptation retains the two-rhyme, opening-phrase return.
The last five-line stanza includes the short refrain.
The opening stanza includes six full lines and the returning fragment at position seven.
Both names are documented for twelve-position arrangements with matching stanza lengths and rhyme letters. Refrain treatment and historical terminology limit interchangeability.

Rondeau redoublé.note: The lines of stanza one successively close stanzas two through five. The final four full lines take an additional short refrain from the opening phrase.

edges.evidence: The first five stanzas have four full lines apiece. The final stanza adds a short returning phrase after four full lines.
The redoubled rondeau expands the reuse of opening material into successive complete end-lines and a final phrase.
A final quatrain and a short returning phrase occupy five positions when the phrase is printed separately.

Rondel.note: The first two lines return mid-poem. Closings can repeat only the first or both openings; the catalog’s 13–14 range is incompatible with requiring only line one in every ending.

edges.evidence: The first two stanzas each have four lines.
The thirteen-line construction ends with a quintain.
The fourteen-line construction ends with a sestet.
The French dictionary classifies the rondel as a rondeau form.
The two opening refrain lines recur as a pair at the end of the second quatrain and again in the fourteen-line version.

Roundel.note: Two four-position stanzas frame a tercet. The returning short phrase comes from the opening line.

edges.evidence: The middle stanza has three lines.
The opening and closing stanzas each have four lines including the short refrain.
The eleven-line English adaptation uses a recurring opening fragment and two rhyme sounds.

Rondelet.note: The same four-syllable line occupies positions 1, 3 and 7; lowercase a and b identify rhyme sounds, not repeated lines.

edges.evidence: All seven positions constitute the single stanza, including a recurring line at positions one, three and seven.

Roundelay.note: The entry describes a general refrain song with no fixed length. The refrain may be one line or two, and no rhyme inside the two-line alternative is specified.

edges.evidence: The two-line refrain alternative pairs its lines deliberately. A one-line refrain is also available.

Triolet.note: Two whole lines reappear on top of two rhyme sounds. Lines 1,4,7 match and lines 2,8 match.

edges.evidence: The eight-line unit realizes the general octave sense. Its ABaAabAB refrain pattern is specific to the triolet.
The forms share recurring words or lines and a two-rhyme inventory.

Ballade.note: Three 8-line stanzas and one 4-line envoi share their final refrain. In the standard form the envoi uses a subset of the stanza rhyme sounds; it does not have to use all three.

edges.evidence: The derived form is Ten-line ballade. Its outgoing assertion supplies the specific-to-general direction. Treating Ballade as the variant would reverse that direction.
The derived form is Double ballade. Its outgoing assertion supplies the specific-to-general direction. Treating Ballade as the variant would reverse that direction.
The derived form is Ballade à double refrain. Its outgoing assertion supplies the specific-to-general direction. Treating Ballade as the variant would reverse that direction.
Each eight-line stanza follows ababbcbC, matching both the generic octave and the ballade huitain scheme.
The envoi has four lines.
The principal eight-line stanzas share ABABBCBC. A ballade repeats its final line as a refrain.

Ten-line ballade.note: Three stanzas share ababbccdcD. The catalog closes with five lines for 35 total. A documented six-line envoi gives 36. Capital D marks the recurring line.

edges.evidence: The inherited stanza-ending refrain remains while the full stanzas and envoi grow to ten and five lines.
The refrain closes a five-line envoi.
The documented ababbccdcD stanza is ababbccdcd when refrain D is counted as its rhyme sound.
One attested alternative ends with a six-line ccdccD envoi.

Double ballade.note: Six stanzas give 48 or 60 lines. An optional envoi yields 52 or 65 in the two documented constructions.

edges.evidence: Six instead of three main stanzas share a refrain.
In the eight-line construction, each of the six principal stanzas is an octave. The ten-line alternative uses a different unit.
In the documented ten-line version, all six principal stanzas use ababbccdcd, the catalogued dizain scheme.
The eight-line construction can end with a four-line envoi. The envoi is optional.
The ten-line construction can end with a five-line envoi. The envoi is optional.

Ballade à double refrain.note: In the historical model, the additional refrain closes the fourth line of each main stanza and the second line of the envoi; the other refrain closes both stanza types.

edges.evidence: The variant adds a second refrain within each stanza and the envoi.
The three eight-line stanzas each carry recurring lines at positions four and eight.
Its envoi repeats the two refrains at positions two and four in a four-line unit.

Chant royal.note: Five matched eleven-line stanzas plus a five-line envoi give 60 lines. All use the same five-rhyme inventory; the refrain closes each stanza. The five-rhyme inventory applies throughout each stanza and is not a span before a refrain.

edges.evidence: Five lines make up the envoi.
Both repeat a stanza-ending refrain and conclude with a shorter envoi. A line of descent is not established.

Virelai.note: The catalog gives the linked-rhyme literary pattern called virelai ancien. A medieval musical virelai instead combines an opening refrain with contrasting music and a return. The two layers are not interchangeable.

edges.evidence: The linked-rhyme literary form carries a short line’s rhyme into the next stanza’s long lines, adapting the lai pattern. This claim concerns that construction.

Virelai nouveau.note: The historical literary description alternates the two opening lines as stanza endings, then closes with both in reverse order. The stanza lengths vary.

edges.evidence: The literary nouveau alternates a two-line refrain. The ancien construction links rhyme sounds across successive stanzas. The common name covers different procedures.
The two opening refrain lines form a unit that returns in reverse order at the end.

Lai.note: The catalog describes a nine-line verse pattern made from three aab units, each of 5, 5 and 2 syllables. This cannot be generalized to all medieval narrative or musical lais.

edges.evidence: In the catalog’s nine-line literary pattern, three AAB groups each contain three lines.

Kyrielle.note: Catalog quatrains have eight syllables per line and a shared refrain in the final position. The sonnet adaptation adds a closing pair.

edges.evidence: Each four-line stanza includes its recurring final line.
Both end successive quatrains on a repeated line.
The three changing eight-syllable lines form the designated opening group of the repeating quatrain, followed by the separate refrain line.

Quatern.note: The first line is repeated at successive local positions 1, 2, 3 and 4 in four quatrains. The row prescribes no rhyme scheme.

edges.evidence: The travelling refrain occurs once in each of four quatrains.

Canzone.note: The catalog’s general outline allows five to seven matching stanzas and a short envoi. Two more specific constructions rotate end-words through five twelve-line stanzas, with either five or six concluding lines.

edges.evidence: The 65-line construction closes with a five-line envoi.
The 66-line historical construction closes with a six-line envoi.

Ballata.note: The source describes an opening ripresa, then two matching parts and a turn back to the recurring refrain. It gives no fixed number of subsequent stanzas.

Stornello.note: One three-line pattern opens with a short line followed by two longer lines. There are also three-long-line and two-line variants, with regional differences in rhyme and assonance.

edges.evidence: The catalog’s stanza and two attested Italian patterns have three lines. Other historical variants have two.
A two-line regional version consists of two rhyming or assonant eleven-syllable lines. This alternative differs from the three-line catalog reading.

Glosa.note: In a strict construction, the four lines of a borrowed epigraph close successive ten-line stanzas. Other traditions retain the line-by-line return while varying the stanza sizes.

edges.evidence: The strict version opens with a four-line borrowed stanza; the ten-line glossing stanzas follow.
Ten-line glosses occur; the catalog’s Décima espinela also demands an exact rhyme order and octosyllabic metre, neither established by the generic Glosa row.
Ten-line units are attested, but the cited definition does not give the specific rhyme sequence of the catalog’s dizain.

Ovillejo.note: Three long-and-short echo pairs precede a four-line stanza. Its last line gathers the three short replies in order; equal metre across a pair is not required.

edges.evidence: Its closing four-line unit ends by assembling the echo words.
Each of three long questions is paired with its own short echo or answer. The two lines within a pair differ in length.

Pantoum.note: The repeating transfer is 2→1 and 4→3 between quatrains. Returning to the opening line is frequent; modern examples vary the rhyme and need not have a circular ending.

edges.evidence: The linked verse units have four lines.
The pantoum adapts the linked Malay pantun tradition into a sequence of interlocking quatrains. The general pantun can also stand alone.

Pantun.note: The common four-line Malay pattern pairs an opening image with the ensuing meaning across ABAB. UNESCO describes four lines as the commonest length, not the only length.

edges.evidence: This particular diagram describes the common four-line variety.
In the four-line pattern, an introductory image occupies one pair and the meaning or answer occupies another. The ABAB sound pattern crosses between the pairs.

Ghazal.note: In the English refrain-bearing pattern, the opening lines and every later second line share rhyme and radif. Five to fifteen is typical, and a poet’s signature is customary rather than mandatory. Signature is a property of the closing couplet, with no assigned first-line position.

edges.evidence: Each autonomous two-line stanza is a couplet. The rhyme and refrain come at both ends of the opening couplet and at the second line of subsequent couplets.

Qasida.note: Nostalgic prelude, journey and final theme supply one conventional order. A bayt consists of two hemistichs within one verse. English layouts can vary.

edges.evidence: Arabic lineation can set one bayt as two hemistichs on the same line. The term couplet also occurs in Persian prosody. These traditions do not establish a two-line English layout.

Haiku.note: Japanese 5–7–5 counts sound units, not English syllables. The Haiku Society of America emphasizes the cut and relationship of images and does not impose three lines or a mandatory English season word. A traditional Japanese template uses 5, 7 and 5 on.

edges.evidence: Both are short verse forms. Their characteristic concerns differ, and an English syllable count alone cannot establish a subtype relationship.

Senryu.note: English senryu often use one to three lines. A human observation is central; humor, a cut, and an English 5–7–5 syllable count are not obligatory.

edges.evidence: Both are short verse forms. Their characteristic concerns differ, and an English syllable count alone cannot establish a subtype relationship.

Tanka.note: Five short lines are common in English, but Japanese 5–7–5–7–7 counts sound units. The English central turn is a frequent expressive move rather than an exact syllabic boundary. The traditional phrase groups have 5, 7, 5, 7 and 7 sound units.

edges.evidence: The common five-line English presentation has the span of a quintain. English lineation varies.
